rows.description: A teenager writes in capitals, many exclamation marks or dramatic emojis, which may be play, real intensity or performing for followers. Tone online is easy to misread, so a quick check helps.

rows.description: A teenager may swing from laughing to irritable to tearful within an hour. Changing moods are common in adolescence, so patient consistency, sleep and gentle talk support balance.

rows.description: A teenager plays feelings down with a shrug or fine to avoid drama. Understatement protects privacy but may hide real need, so trusted adults leave the door open.

rows.description: A teenager laughs loudly after a slip in front of others, covering embarrassment. Others may read it as confidence, and the laugh may be relief or fear of rejection.

rows.description: A teenager laughs off a hurtful joke to avoid looking weak. The smile is protection, and a friend may gently follow up privately, never assume, and offer support.

rows.description: A young adult studying or working abroad finds that how openly faces show emotion differs across cultures and families; a restrained face may be respect or calm, not coldness. Asking directly avoids stereotypes.

rows.description: A young adult reads faces through lag, small screens and frozen frames, where a frown may be a bad connection or concentration. Checking in verbally is more reliable than inferring mood from a paused face.

rows.description: A young adult tells a polite, mouth-only smile from a warm, sustained smile that also involves the eyes, but treats the difference as a rough clue only, since many genuine smiles are quiet and many polite ones are convincing.

rows.description: A student in a new city finds smiling at strangers is friendly in some places and odd in others; a smile can also cover embarrassment or apology, as in parts of Asia. Local norms matter more than assumptions.

rows.description: A young adult in an interview raises the brows to show interest and avoids furrowing them when nervous. Interviewers should remember that a tense forehead may only signal effort or anxiety.
